subject: giant prehistoric rodent
title: Two Teeth From a Coal Mine Revealed a 66-Pound Rat From 34 Million Years Ago

scenes.text: A geologist picked up what she thought was a bone. It was a rat's tooth.
A rat the size of a medium dog. Around 30 kilograms, 66 pounds, from a coal mine in southern Thailand.
It lived about 34 million years ago, twice the size of any other rodent known from that time.
Only two teeth were found: a molar and one incisor. From their size, scientists worked out the whole animal.
They named it Yakamys, from the Thai word for giant, and published it in November 2026.
Today's biggest rodent, the capybara, is about twice as heavy. Giant rats, it turns out, started in Asia.

description:
A geologist picked up what she thought was a bone. It was a rat's tooth.
The two teeth, a molar and an incisor from a lignite mine in Krabi Province, southern Thailand, belonged to a rodent of roughly 30 kilograms (66 pounds) that lived about 34 million years ago, about twice the size of other known rodents of its time. Researchers from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources and French universities named it Yakamys sirindhornae in Scientific Reports in November 2026. The modern capybara, the largest living rodent, is about twice as heavy.
What would you do if a dog-sized rat ran past you?
first_comment: The teeth were dug up in 2004 and sat unidentified for over 20 years. Which extinct animal would you least like to meet alive?
